Being around people in authority or uniform

Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

People are not what they seem

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a refugee trauma profile, comments on sexual violence are too trauma-specific and suggest a sexual assault formulation that is not otherwise supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. Nothing else in the profile indicates sexual trauma content, making this trigger hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding situations where others evaluate appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers on danger, distrust, intrusive sensory recall, and hypervigilance rather than evaluation-based threat. This strategy is not well linked to the active trigger/threat/appraisal pattern and is clinically out of place.

vignette:
Marisol Alvarez is a 34-year-old married woman who came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to handle things on her own. She works as a prison guard, a job she once took pride in for its structure and steadiness, but she now moves through her shifts with a constant sense that danger can break through at any moment. The fear feels familiar to her. It reaches back to the period when, as a young woman fleeing violence and instability in her home country, she traveled with family members and other refugees under the control of armed men and local officials who decided where people stood, sat, waited, and moved. One night that remains sharply fixed in her mind, the group was stopped in a crowded holding area by uniformed men shouting instructions. The air was sour with sweat and alcohol. Marisol remembers the slurred voice of one guard barking orders, the sound of boots scraping, people crying, and the way everyone around her became instantly obedient because disobedience felt unthinkable. She can still hear those commands in her head as if they are happening beside her.

She describes that memory as painfully clear, not blurred by time. When it returns, it does not feel like a distant story she is recounting but like a scene that arrives in full detail, with the shouted words and harsh tones coming back first. If she tries to say more once it starts, she quickly becomes flooded and has to stop. In early sessions she would begin to describe the holding area, then fall silent, press her hands together, and say that she could hear them again. What frightened her most was not only what had happened then, but how easily the feeling of helplessness still took over her body now.

Over the years, she had come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that people are not what they seem. She notices herself scanning others for signs of hidden threat, especially anyone wearing a uniform or giving directions in a clipped, authoritative tone. This has become particularly difficult in her workplace. At the prison, uniforms are everywhere, including her own, and orders are part of every shift briefing. When a supervisor gives a sudden instruction from behind her or an inmate moves abruptly in her peripheral vision, Marisol reacts before she has time to think, with a jolt of alarm that leaves her heart racing and her muscles tight. She knows, afterward, that nothing has actually happened, but in the moment her body is certain she is in immediate danger.

She has adapted her days around this sense of threat. In the staff room she chooses seats with a wall behind her and a clear view of the door. In meetings she positions herself where no one can approach unseen. At home, in restaurants or family gatherings, she does the same, to the point that her husband has noticed she cannot simply sit wherever there is space. Unexpected movement nearby can make her flinch hard enough to embarrass her, and she is left feeling exposed and ashamed, as if she has revealed something she cannot control.

Certain sensory cues are especially potent. The smell of alcohol can instantly pull her back to that night with the uniformed men, especially if it comes off someone’s breath unexpectedly. At work, if she catches that smell on a coworker during the end of a shift, she becomes tense and watchful for the rest of the hour. To manage what happens inside her, she often turns up loud music or the television when she gets home, trying to drown out the replay of voices in her head. She also keeps her distance from authority figures when she can, limiting casual contact with supervisors and avoiding situations where she might be singled out or directly instructed unless absolutely necessary. This has begun to affect her standing at work; she worries she seems difficult or detached, though to her it feels safer not to be too visible.

When she cannot sleep, she dwells on how the event might have been prevented, mentally reworking each choice and each moment of obedience, as if there had been some correct action that would have changed everything. These thoughts leave her exhausted and no more settled. She says she no longer feels like the person she was before all of this, or even the person she expected to become in adulthood. The uniform she wears for work adds another layer of disorientation: sometimes she catches sight of herself and feels like she has become part of something she once feared.

What finally brought Marisol to seek help was a recent incident at work when a supervisor called out a sharp instruction and another officer moved suddenly at her side; she spun and recoiled so dramatically that several colleagues stared. Afterward she sat in her car shaking, overwhelmed by the sound of the command still echoing in her mind. She came to treatment frightened by how quickly she can feel transported into danger, and hoping, cautiously, that she might find a way to live in her marriage, her work, and her own body without always bracing for the next threat.
